catalog_citation: Hill, Jane H. & Kenneth C. Hill. 2019. Comparative Takic Grammar. Survey of California and Other Indian Languages, Report 17. Berkeley: University of California. 1475 pp. Open access, eScholarship item qt6tr732gg (https://escholarship.org/uc/item/6tr732gg).

catalog_quote: [p. 92, sec. 3.4] A major distinction among the groups is that in TV and the Serran languages, the domain for stress is the word. ... A short vowel counts as one mora and long vowel as two moras for the placement of stress. In Takic, syllable-final consonants also figure in the mora count ... TV and SE share a system of stress on the syllable containing the second mora of the word, including any prefixes. SE and KI also, unlike TV, have stress on the first syllable of the word even if it is short, at least in citation forms. This means for SE, and probably as well for KI, that both a short first syllable and the second syllable are in strong position, with subsequent syllables being pronounced in a much more reduced fashion, often losing a short vowel entirely when followed by an obstruent consonant. ... In context, initial short syllables tend not to be stressed and they may weaken; an extreme case has been noted with chichint ‘boy’, which in fast speech has been heard as chchint or even as just chint. [p. 95] 3.4.2. SERRANO STRESS. In SE, the first two moras are in “strong” position. This gives the impression of stress on the first syllable if it is long (contains a long vowel (1a,b), or is closed by a consonant (1c‑e)), and on both the first and second syllables if the first syllable is short (1f-k). ... An underlyingly final syllable is normally extrametrical.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word-level (prefixes included), left-edge, quantity-sensitive: the first two moras of the word are metrically strong (long vowels = 2 moras; coda consonants also count). If the first syllable is heavy (long vowel or closed) it alone carries the stress; if it is light, both the first and the second syllable are stressed (second-mora stress plus initial prominence in citation forms). Later syllables are weak and reduce/syncopate; an underlyingly word-final syllable is extrametrical.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Authors say little is known about secondary stress and describe only primary stress (p. 92), but note that strong and weak positions alternate through the word after the initial two-mora window: 'A syllable after a weak syllable is again in strong position. There is in effect an alternating secondary stress' (sec. 4.2.3, p. 147); non-initial closed or long-vowel syllables also count as strong (p. 92).
new_statements.exceptions: Underlyingly final syllable is extrametrical (p. 95); for verbs, stem-final syllables and inflectional endings appear to remain extrametrical (p. 96); in connected speech initial short syllables tend not to be stressed and may weaken (chichint > chchint > chint, p. 92); Spanish loans conform (kjaleesa7 'buggy', p. 95).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word including prefixes (contrast with Cupan languages where prefixes are extrametrical). Initial-syllable stress on a light first syllable is stated to hold 'at least in citation forms'. Data are K. C. Hill's own Serrano fieldwork (Morongo Reservation, 1963-64 onward) plus Harrington and Ramón & Elliott 2000 materials.
new_statements.identity_note: Both sources describe Serrano proper (serr1255) as recorded chiefly from Morongo Reservation speakers (Sarah Morongo Martin, Louie Marcus; later Dorothy Ramón) by K. C. Hill from 1963 on; Hill & Hill 2019 abbreviate it SE and treat it together with Kitanemuk (kita1245, KI) as 'Serran', but sec. 3.4.2 is specifically Serrano. Note the Glottolog 'grammar' list for serr1255 is polluted by two Iberoromania book reviews (authors surnamed Serrano) and by Anderton 1988, which is a Kitanemuk grammar.
